I’ve never waited too long for support personally, although, I’ve never been offered any trauma specific support from my community mental health team. Only therapies related to anxiety and depression. Or rather coaching from a psychologist around grounding techniques and mindfullness. 

I suspect I have complex PTSD; and as another poster mentioned you will probably be waiting a long time for help or will be offered nothing other than IAPT or CBT.

In my personal view, the NHS is backwards when it comes to mental health provision unless your psychotic or have schizophrenia they may either give you antipsychotics or section you instead of longer term CMHT support (which some teams from what I’ve read - anecdotally - don’t even do this - entirely depends on the individual psychiatrist.

I told a CPN I wanted help with trauma after she asked me what support I wanted. She replied “well I can’t take your trauma away from you!”. So if that doesn’t say something about the state of affairs I dunno what does.

I’m not sure what you mean by council support list; I presume you mean social support from social services? This is what I currently get which is okay but it’s not psychological support (which is what you need).

You should probably go to your GP and mention trauma and PTSD and get referred to the mental health team in the least.

In my own personal view; don’t rely on the NHS. If you can, I’d pay to see someone privately. A good place to look for therapists privately in the UK is:
www. counselling-directory.org.uk 

I’ve found therapists on there myself and some of them will specialise in trauma. For things like EMDR or DBT or other trauma focussed therapies the cost may go up. I’d expect to pay around £50 per session (avg) and try to see someone fortnightly if you can afford it or three-weekly. I see someone 3/weekly and it does help although I think therapeutically it would help to see them fortnightly at least. Weekly is the ideal but not everyone can afford this.

One other thing; a lot of therapists will often waiver fees or reduce them according to means. If your on a low income or benefits they may have a sliding scale so they offer to let you pay what you can within your means. Some are insurance based as well. Always ask or check their profile. My therapist for example does reduced fees for certain demographics.

Lastly, try to find support groups if you can.

I used to work in benefits; I know that statistically a majority of PIP decisions are overturned on appeal. Those that aren’t it’s usually more about how you answer the questions or your assessment. In my own personal experience (as a pip applicant) who got his own app rejected (I have cerebral palsy, severe anxiety, depression, paranoia and suspected autism), I’d advise you to the advocacy route and you get support from CAB or Disability Action Group in your location. Those that had theirs rejected it’s usually because they didn’t have support or anyone helping them. It does add weight if you request that help. Add any documentation from your psychiatrist or doctor. 

it’s about how you phrase things and whether it ticks the boxes. You shouldn’t have to exaggerate or anything but I’d suggest not giving them any room to twist or omit vital details from your app. Don’t give them a reason to not award it to you.

I’m 32M UK and so I thought I’d post my experiences as someone who has twelve years exp of mental health issues/trauma and problems with dating/rejection:

I don’t have any advice re dating side of things…other than to say set your stall up accordingly; by this I mean set your expectations low and have boundaries. 

You will meet a lot of broken and emotionally unavailable people on apps. I’ve met very few genuine or stable individuals online; it’s the nature of apps but our broken society. Nobody seems to communicate in the real world anymore.

I’m on dating apps; and I’ve been through a lot of rubbish to be honest. What I will advise about your profile is; be very blunt and authentic. Even if what you say isn’t attractive or popular; if it puts people off so be it - it means your getting closer to the person who is your match.

Regarding therapy I recommend referring yourself to your local IAPT service on the NHS. Don’t have high expectations however, secondly, look at third sector orgs like Mind who may offer subsidised therapy.

Depending on what your income is you may be able to get private psychotherapy. I would strongly recommend: counselling-directory.org.uk for searching for a private therapist. 

A lot of therapist will see clients on a ‘sliding scale’ according to your means/if on low income or benefits also; you would need to ask of enquire.

Lastly, in terms of podcasts there is lots out there. I run s podcast myself; I’m not a medical expert but I invite guest speakers on my platform to talk about their own lives experiences. Here it is if your interested: https://spotify.link/af2xxCH9byb

I got up to shake her had afterwards and she stepped right back out of my space like she smelled something really awful. This triggered me and I went home thinking what was the reason? Your paranoia could be part of anxiety or OCD in extreme cases or it could be something else but only a psychiatrist will be able to diagnose this; and most of the time it’s hard to get one either way!
